source.title: Unpacking Large Language Models with Conceptual Consistency
source.authors: Pritish Sahu; Michael Cogswell; Yun-Ye Gong; Ajay Divakaran

record.tranche_reason: It evaluates CommonsenseQA performance across language-model sizes, a different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling, and reports an explicit size trend relevant to V6.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit scaling laws, extrapolate from smaller runs, or test compute-optimal allocation. Its model-scale results for conceptual consistency are recorded as a related but distinct construct. Relation- and concept-specific consistency plots and background-fact accuracy are not rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates zero-shot CommonsenseQA accuracy across 10 checkpoints from three families (125M to 66B) and reports that accuracy rises with size. That result bears on V6 in a new setting. It fits no scaling relation and does not use pretraining loss, so the test of predictability is only qualitative. T3 fits better than T2 because scale is not the study's question; it reports the trend as an expected side result.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that LLMs have moderate conceptual consistency that increases with scale and varies across relations, concepts and prompts. The paraphrase omits one conclusion: background knowledge grows much less with scale than task accuracy or consistency, which the authors read as evidence of a skill hierarchy.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates zero-shot CommonsenseQA and predicts correctness from ConceptNet background-question scores; it does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Conceptual-consistency results vary across relations, concepts, and prompts; the authors also report a plateau between OPT-30B and OPT-66B. They note that prompts were not designed specifically for T0.

fits_no_version.finding: Conceptual consistency (average precision of predicting CSQA correctness from background-knowledge scores) generally rises with scale in all families. OPT-30B and OPT-66B do not differ, and T0 is much lower.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistency between a model's background knowledge and its QA correctness rises with model scale, with possible diminishing returns.

record.problems: The study uses one question-answering dataset's development set and does not test pretraining loss or fit predictive scaling relationships. Many plotted values are not given numerically in the text. The authors say the OPT-30B to OPT-66B performance increases may not be significant; the stated 95% confidence intervals concern background-knowledge performance, not the plotted anchor-task accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: Relation- and concept-specific conceptual-consistency breakdowns (Figures 5 and 7) are not separately extracted because they are subsets of the related construct recorded in r11-r20 and do not measure a listed claim version. Background-fact accuracy and prompt-bias comparisons (Figures 4a and 6) are also omitted because they are not downstream task performance or any other outcome named by the versions.

untested.parts: No fitted predictive relation (power law or otherwise), no pretraining loss as a predictor, no extrapolation to larger models, only one downstream task (CSQA dev set).
No shape comparison at fixed size.
No other modalities or regimes tested for power-law form.

missing.what: Background-fact verification accuracy (balanced yes/no ConceptNet facts, averaged over 14 relations, with 95% CI) rises with model size but over a smaller range than CSQA accuracy. This is a second downstream-style measure of scale trends.
missing.locator: Figure 4a; Section 5 'Background and Task Performance'; Conclusions

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is weak and qualitative: figure-only values, one dataset, no fit. Comparisons across families (e.g. T0 below OPT/GPT) reflect model family and training differences, not scale, and do not bear on V6. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law behavior in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested for power-law scaling.
The study reports zero-shot CommonsenseQA accuracy across model sizes, but does not fit a predictive relation, test pretraining loss as a predictor, or examine other downstream tasks.
No fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across setup or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: OPT 350M–30B, GPT(EleutherAI) 125M–6B and T0 3B–11B on zero-shot CSQA dev accuracy
relationships.reason: Text states anchor-task accuracy increases with model size within each family (Fig 4b). Values are figure-only, so the verdict rests on the text. Rows r1-r4, r6-r10.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased with model size within each tested family.

relationships.reason: The authors call the task gain 'marginal' and possibly not significant, a possible plateau at the top of the range (r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: The gain from OPT-30B to OPT-66B was marginal and potentially insignificant, suggesting a plateau.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
